summary: A progress report from Rand on checking which ARPANET sites had been tested against the early protocols. The table notes whether each host handled the host-host protocol basics, the initial connection protocol, and Telnet as user and server. It warns that these were one-time arranged tests, not a measure of ongoing availability.

plainLanguage.summary: This report records which functions were checked at listed ARPANET sites as of August 21. It warns that the checks were limited and do not show whether a site was continuously available.

subtitle: A dated report of protocol checks performed on ARPANET hosts in August 1971.

tldr.problem: Users needed to know which ARPANET hosts had passed checks for basic network and Telnet functions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC tabulates verification marks by host and explains what the NCP, ICP and Telnet columns do and do not show.
tldr.outcome: The checks were arranged one-time tests and do not indicate continuous availability.

today: RFC 214 is a dated network checkout report from August 1971. The unit metadata says it obsoletes RFC 198.

sections.title: The Checkout Table
sections.content:
As of August 21, the author reported arranged verifications for listed ARPANET sites. The table covers NCP-107, ICP-156, user Telnet, server Telnet, Logger and Access Service, with marks for verified, not applicable and entries with comments.

The listed sites include UCLA Sigma7, SRI NIC, UCSB, BBN, MIT, SDC, Lincoln and Utah.
sections.plainLanguage: The table records whether selected functions were checked at each site. It is a snapshot of those checks, not a complete inventory.

sections.title: What the NCP Check Means
sections.content:
The author says the NCP-107 heading is misleading if read as a full test of NCP functions. It only means the NCP responded to RESET, which Rand's NCP needed to consider a remote host up, and performed functions needed for an ICP.

Functions such as ECHO, Give Back and error-message generation were not checked exhaustively. Some were checked with UCSB and SDC.
sections.plainLanguage: An NCP mark means a limited set of checks passed. It does not mean every NCP function was tested.

sections.title: Comments and Follow-up
sections.content:
The RFC reports that SRI NIC had a server Telnet and logger that did not process Telnet messages correctly. At MIT Multics, the authors reached an interim logger that sent a 'ts' message; at SDC, the logger caused a crash after login.

The author asks that discrepancies be reported by phone and says the RFC would be updated in about one month.
sections.plainLanguage: The comments describe a few specific problems with logins and Telnet processing. The report invites corrections by phone.
